title: Oil Spill Vulnerability in the Arabian/Persian Gulf Threatens Regional Water Security and Global Energy Supply
content:
Abstract

The Arabian/Persian Gulf contains more than half of the world's proven oil reserves and is a critical hub for global energy transport, yet it faces increasing oil spill risk from intense tanker traffic, geopolitical tensions, and clandestine oil smuggling operations. At the same time, the region is among the most water-scarce globally and relies heavily on seawater desalination, making desalination plants and oil and gas (O&G) export terminals highly vulnerable to marine oil pollution. Here we combine backward-in-time oil spill dispersal simulations for 2016–2022 with marine traffic data to identify offshore areas from which spills are most likely to impact these infrastructures. Oil spill vulnerability shows strong seasonal variability, with northwesterly Shamal winds driving pollution toward the southeastern Gulf, particularly affecting facilities in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Qatar. Two major high-risk zones emerge: a southwestern corridor linking Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Bahrain, and the UAE, and a northeastern hotspot along the UAE coastline. We find that about 19% of the Gulf's surface constitutes a high-risk area from which spilled oil could reach key water or energy infrastructures in less than 3 days. These short transport times highlight the limited window for spill detection and response and underscore the need for improved monitoring, forecasting, and international coordination.
